subject: Geography
board: National Curriculum (KS1-3), aligned to AQA GCSE 9-1
source: National Curriculum (KS1 geography: local area, UK countries, weather, simple maps); school Geography resources reviewed for ethos and stewardship links

lessons.unit: Unit 1: My place in the world
lessons.title: My home, my school and my local area
objectives: Name places we can find in our local area
Say if something is natural or made by people
Say one way to look after our area

keywords.def: the streets and places close to where we live
made by nature, not by people, like a tree or a river
built or made by people, like a house or a road
a place where Muslims pray together

starter: Say Bismillah. Tell me one thing you can see from your window.
What is the name of the country we live in?
Is your home a house or a flat? Show me with your hands how big it is.

teach.heading: Where do we live?
bullets: We all live in a home.
Our home is in a street, a town or a city.
The streets and places near us are our local area.
teach.note: Start with Bismillah. Hold up a picture or drawing of a street. Ask: what is near your home? Take answers from children and write them on the screen. Keep it concrete: do not worry about names of towns, just near/far.

teach.heading: Places in a local area
bullets: Many areas have a shop, a park and a school.
Many areas have a masjid, a library and a bus stop.
Each place has a job. A shop sells things.
teach.note: Show 6 photos of typical UK places (shop, park, school, masjid, library, bus stop). For each, ask 'What do people do here?' Praise full sentences. Misconception: some children think the local area means only their own house.

teach.heading: Natural or made by people?
bullets: Natural things: trees, grass, rivers, hills.
Made by people: houses, roads, shops, bridges.
Allah created the natural world for us to look after.
teach.note: Play 'Natural / Made' on screen: show 8 pictures, children show thumbs up for natural and hands on head for made. A garden is a good tricky one: the plants are natural but the garden was planned by people. Accept either answer with a reason.

teach.heading: Looking after our area
bullets: We put litter in the bin.
We do not pick flowers in the park.
The Prophet (peace be upon him): cleanliness is half of faith (Sahih Muslim).
teach.note: Link care for the local area to adab. Ask: what could we do this week to keep our street clean? Note: you are citing the well-known hadith about cleanliness; keep it simple and say it plainly.

practice: Look at the picture of a street. Point to one natural thing and one man-made thing.
Tell your partner: 'In my area there is a ___.' Say it three different ways.
independent: Draw your home in the middle of a page. Draw and label three places near it.
Colour the natural things green and the man-made things blue in the picture sheet.
Stretch: add one thing that you would like in your local area and say why.
exit: Name one place in your local area.
Is a river natural or man-made?
lessons.homework: Walk or look around your street with an adult and draw or photograph two natural things and two man-made things.
lessons.send: Use real photos and word cards with pictures; allow children to point or draw answers. EAL: say each place name together and show the picture. Stretch: ask children to explain why a place is useful.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: My place in the world
lessons.title: Our United Kingdom: four countries
objectives: Name the four countries of the United Kingdom
Match each country to its capital city
Find the UK on a map

keywords.def: a land with its own name, borders and people
the most important city in a country
four countries joined together: England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland
a drawing that shows where places are

starter: Say Bismillah. Name one place near our homes.
Is a hill natural or made by people?
Can you remember what we call the streets and places near us?

teach.heading: The United Kingdom
bullets: We live in the United Kingdom, or UK.
The UK is made of four countries.
They are England, Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.
teach.note: Show a coloured map of the UK with the four countries in four colours. Say each name and ask children to echo. Many children think England and the UK are the same thing. Say clearly: England is one country inside the UK.

teach.heading: Capital cities
bullets: England's capital is London.
Scotland's capital is Edinburgh.
Wales has Cardiff. Northern Ireland has Belfast.
teach.note: Use a chant with actions: 'England, London. Scotland, Edinburgh. Wales, Cardiff. Northern Ireland, Belfast.' Do it three times, getting faster. Ask who has been to one of the cities.

teach.heading: Looking at a map
bullets: England is the biggest country in the UK.
Scotland is in the north. Wales is in the west.
A map shows us where each country is.
teach.note: Use the words north, south, east, west only lightly. Point to England at the bottom, Scotland at the top. Ask children to point on their own drawn map with a finger on their screen.

teach.heading: Flags of the UK
bullets: Each country has its own flag.
The Union Flag joins them together.
Flags are symbols. They tell us about a place.
teach.note: Show the four national flags and the Union Flag. Ask children to spot colours. You do not need to explain the history of the crosses at this age. Keep the focus on 'each country is different but they are joined together'.

practice: Together on screen: drag each capital city label to the right country.
Say the sentence: 'The capital of ___ is ___.' for each country.
independent: Colour the four countries of the UK map in four different colours and write their names.
Match each capital city to its country with a line.
Stretch: draw a flag for one of the countries and say why you chose the colours.
exit: Name the four countries of the UK.
What is the capital city of England?
lessons.homework: Ask someone at home which country they or their family were born in, and find it on a world map or globe.
lessons.send: Provide a UK outline with country names already placed for support. EAL: use flag cards and repeat the chant with actions. Stretch: ask which country is the smallest and which is the biggest.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: My place in the world
lessons.title: Weather and the four seasons in the UK
objectives: Name the four seasons in order
Say what the weather is often like in autumn and winter

keywords.def: what the sky and air are like outside today
one of four parts of the year: spring, summer, autumn, winter
the season when leaves fall and days get shorter
how hot or cold it is

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four countries of the UK.
What is the capital city of England?
What is the weather like outside today? Tell your partner.

teach.heading: What is weather?
bullets: Weather is what it is like outside.
It can be sunny, cloudy, rainy, windy, snowy or foggy.
Weather can change in one day.
teach.note: Show weather symbols one by one and ask children to act out each (shiver for cold, flap hands for wind). Ask: what did you wear today and why? This links weather to everyday life.

teach.heading: The four seasons
bullets: The year has four seasons.
They are spring, summer, autumn and winter.
They come round in the same order every year.
teach.note: Show a season wheel. Say the seasons in order and count on fingers. We are in autumn now (November). Ask: what is the next season? Many children will say 'Christmas' or 'Ramadan' - gently bring them back to 'winter'.

teach.heading: Autumn and winter in the UK
bullets: In autumn leaves change colour and fall.
In winter it is cold. Days are short.
We wear coats, hats and scarves.
teach.note: Show photographs of the same park in each season. Ask: what is different? Encourage descriptive words (brown, bare, frosty). Mention that daylight is shorter in winter, so it gets dark early, which affects the times of prayer.

teach.heading: Spring and summer in the UK
bullets: In spring flowers grow and it gets warmer.
In summer it is warm and the days are long.
We wear T-shirts and sun hats.
teach.note: Link to the idea that the sun is higher in the sky in summer. Do not go into the reasons why seasons happen; just notice and describe. Ask who has a favourite season and why.

practice: Look at four photographs. Say which season each picture shows and how you know.
Choose the right clothes for a rainy autumn day. Explain your choice.
independent: Draw a picture of an autumn day. Add three weather or season words.
Cut and stick the four seasons in the right order.
Stretch: write one sentence about your favourite season.
exit: What is the weather often like in winter in the UK?
lessons.homework: Look outside for three days and draw the weather symbol for each day.
lessons.send: Give a word bank with pictures. EAL: practise weather words with actions. Stretch: ask children to compare summer and winter using the word 'but'.

lessons.unit: Unit 1: My place in the world
lessons.title: Making a simple map
objectives: Explain what a map is for
Use pictures and symbols to show places on a simple map
Make a simple map of the classroom or bedroom

keywords.def: a drawing of a place seen from above
a small picture or sign that stands for something
a box that explains what the symbols on a map mean
the way you go from one place to another

starter: Say Bismillah. Name the four seasons in order.
What are the four countries of the UK?
What is the weather like today? Show me with an action.

teach.heading: What is a map?
bullets: A map is a drawing of a place from above.
It helps us find places and find our way.
A map uses symbols, not full pictures.
teach.note: Show a bird's-eye photograph of a school next to a simple drawn map of the same school. Ask: what is the same and what is different? Introduce the idea that we look straight down from above. Hold a book flat and look down on it.

teach.heading: Symbols and a key
bullets: A symbol is a small sign for something real.
A tree can be a green circle. A road can be a grey line.
A key tells us what each symbol means.
teach.note: Build a simple key together on screen: green circle = tree, blue square = water, red square = house. Check understanding by asking what a blue square means. Misconception: children think symbols have to look exactly like the object.

teach.heading: A map of our room
bullets: Think of the room as seen from the ceiling.
Draw the door, the table and the window.
Use a symbol for each and make a key.
teach.note: Model drawing a map of your own classroom on the screen. Narrate each decision: where is the door? Is the table near the window? Use words such as next to, behind, in front. Let children tell you where to add things.

teach.heading: A route on a map
bullets: A route is the way from one place to another.
Use words: forward, left, right, turn.
Draw a line to show the route on the map.
teach.note: On your map, draw a route from the door to the window. Describe it with left and right. Left and right are tricky at this age: say 'my left hand has the ring' or hold up the L shape with the left hand.

practice: Look at a map of a park. Find the pond, the swings and the café using the key.
Say a route from the gate to the swings using forward, left, right.
independent: Draw a simple map of your bedroom or classroom from above.
Make a key with at least three symbols.
Stretch: draw a route from the door to your favourite place and describe it.
exit: What is a key on a map for?
Draw a symbol for a tree.
lessons.homework: Draw a map of the route from your bedroom to the kitchen. Add a key with two symbols.
lessons.send: Provide a printed outline of the room with spaces for symbols. EAL: label objects in two languages if helpful. Stretch: add a compass arrow showing north.
